rv.q: In Baker’s brilliant The Antipodes (given its UK premiere at the National Theatre), the hunt for plot turns into a quest. Her characters sit around a vast, empty table, trying to dream up an original yarn.
‘The Antipodes’ – which has its UK premiere in a production co-directed by Baker herself and designer Chloe Lamford – is utterly, gloriously out there and will doubtless horrify some people.
Its disquieting mood lingers long, long after its abrupt snap ending.

You know you just have to surrender and go with the flow (and sometimes the lack of it). This time we're in a very handsomely appointed conference room in an unnamed place, where a gathering of six co-workers (five men, one woman) are barnstorming ideas for an unspecified purpose with their boss (who becomes increasingly absent from the proceedi...
This is an ineffectual production of a limp idea.

cn.t: Annie Baker's most surreal work to date divides with its out-there premise about storytelling, but critics largely embrace the bold departure, praising its exploration of narrative and memory in hard times.
